title: Boba or Bubble Tea: What Tapioca Pearls Are and How They Are Made

seo.title: Boba and Bubble Tea: What Tapioca Pearls Are
seo.meta_description: Classic boba pearls are made mainly from tapioca starch derived from cassava. Cooking gelatinizes the starch, creating their elastic, chewy texture.
seo.search_intent: Understand what boba and bubble tea mean, what tapioca pearls are made from, why they are chewy, and how they are cooked before going into drinks.

excerpt: Classic boba pearls are small balls made mainly from tapioca starch, which comes from cassava. When boiled, the starch gelatinizes into a translucent, elastic, chewy structure. The cooked pearls are commonly sweetened and added to milk tea, fruit tea, or other drinks.
content_html:
Classic boba pearls are chewy balls made primarily from tapioca starch, a starch extracted from cassava. They are cooked in water until the starch gelatinizes, creating the elastic, sticky-chewy texture that contrasts with the drink around them.

“Boba” can refer to the pearls themselves or more broadly to the beverage. Bubble tea developed in Taiwan in the 1980s and became known as iced or milk tea served with pearls through an oversized straw.

Tapioca comes from cassava

Cassava roots contain a large amount of starch. Once extracted and dried, the starch can be rehydrated and formed into small spheres. Food databases list tapioca starch balls as cassava-derived products.

Tapioca is not wheat flour and is naturally gluten-free, although commercial pearls can contain additional ingredients, so labels still matter when someone has a strict dietary restriction.

Why are tapioca pearls so chewy?

Tapioca starch has a high proportion of amylopectin and gelatinizes at a relatively low temperature. When heated with water, its starch granules absorb liquid, swell, and form a cohesive network.

Food-science studies specifically describe springiness and chewiness as defining sensory characteristics of tapioca pearls used in bubble tea.

Why are many boba pearls black?

Pure tapioca starch is pale or white. Dark color commonly comes from brown sugar, caramel, molasses, or added coloring incorporated into the dough or later syrup.

A black pearl therefore does not come from a black cassava variety. Clear, white, colored, and flavored pearls are also available.

How are dried tapioca pearls cooked?

Commercial pearls are usually boiled in plenty of water. Timing varies substantially with size and whether they are traditional or quick-cook pearls, so package directions should take priority over one universal time.

During cooking, the exterior becomes translucent and the hard center gradually disappears. Pearls are then commonly rested, drained or rinsed, and mixed with syrup both for sweetness and to reduce sticking.

Not every bubble-tea “ball” is tapioca

Popping boba is a different product. It has a thin gel membrane around liquid and bursts when bitten. It is made using gelling or spherification techniques rather than the same starch structure as tapioca pearls.

Coconut jelly, aloe, puddings, and other inclusions are common too. Ordering “boba” often means tapioca pearls by default, but toppings are not all made the same way.

What else goes into bubble tea?

The base can be black, green, or oolong tea, but modern versions also use fruit drinks and non-tea bases. Milk, plant-based drinks, syrups, fruit, and sweeteners vary by recipe.

As a result, nutrition varies enormously. One drink may contain relatively little added sugar while another gets substantial sugar from syrup, condensed milk, and sweetened pearls.

Tapioca pearls change texture as they sit

Freshly cooked pearls are soft and elastic. As they cool and sit, starch molecules reorganize and texture can become firmer. This is one reason boba shops often cook multiple batches during the day.

At home, prepare roughly what you plan to consume and follow product storage guidance. Refrigeration can accelerate firming in some cooked starches even though cold storage may be necessary when pearls are part of a perishable prepared drink.

The practical rule: classic boba is tapioca starch shaped into pearls and cooked until gelatinized. Starch creates the chewy texture; dark color and sweetness usually come from added ingredients.

faq.question: What is boba made from?
faq.answer: Classic pearls are made mainly from tapioca starch derived from cassava and water, often with sugar or coloring.

faq.question: Why is boba so chewy?
faq.answer: Tapioca starch gelatinizes during cooking and forms an elastic, amylopectin-rich structure.

faq.question: Does bubble tea always contain tea?
faq.answer: Not anymore. The format began with tea, but modern versions can use milk, fruit, and other beverage bases.
